architectural_implications.after: Roadmaps ordered by whether an automatic, objective, self-contained checker exists for the domain; verifier construction becomes the first workstream.
architectural_implications.before: Capability roadmaps and agent investment ordered by perceived domain hardness or size of the prize.
architectural_implications.consequence: The scarce engineering asset shifts from model access or prompting to harnesses, formal specs, and deterministic checkers, and teams without a checker should build one before scaling generation.
architectural_implications.observation: Verifier quality, not domain difficulty, predicts the order in which AI absorbs a field.

architectural_implications.after: Humans own agenda, framing, and accountability; the AI owns proof/lemma/search execution.
architectural_implications.before: Humans authored and executed the artifact; the tool generated suggestions.
architectural_implications.consequence: Tooling must expose objective setting, framing constraints, critique, and ownership assignment — not just raw output — and evaluation must test whether a human can still certify a result they did not derive.
architectural_implications.observation: The human's enforced interface with the AI moves up a level.

architectural_implications.after: Disclosure sections and conceptualization-versus-execution splits become standard parts of the published or shipped artifact.
architectural_implications.before: Authorship and credit assumed a human author of every claim.
architectural_implications.consequence: Trace capture (which model, which prompt, which verifier, which human approver) becomes a required output of the pipeline rather than optional telemetry, and downstream reward/credit systems must be rebuilt on top of it.
architectural_implications.observation: AI assistance forces per-claim provenance into the artifact itself.

article_ideas.based_on: Roadmaps ordered by whether an automatic, objective, self-contained checker exists for the domain; verifier construction becomes the first workstream.
article_ideas.thesis: The domains AI absorbs fastest are the ones with cheap, objective, self-contained validity checking, not the ones that look hardest; therefore the primary engineering artifact in an agentic stack is the checker, and teams should build or buy a deterministic checker before scaling generation.
article_ideas.title: Build the Checker First: Verifier Quality, Not Task Difficulty, Sets the AI Roadmap

article_ideas.angle: Architecture argument with a capacity-planning corollary: budget for verification, deduplication, and human adjudication queues, and instrument the funnel rather than the generator.
article_ideas.audience: Agent framework builders and infrastructure engineers who own throughput and cost budgets.

article_ideas.title: The Funnel Is the Bottleneck: Why Agent Harnesses Should Fan Out Against a Falsifier

article_ideas.angle: Move from the observed rise of AI disclosure sections in papers to a concrete per-claim provenance schema (generator, verifier, human approver, confidence) and argue that the same schema is what makes production agent traces auditable and blame-assignable.

connections.relationship: Enabler — automatic objective validity checking supplies the reward signal that makes RL tractable, so verifier quality determines how fast a domain is absorbed.
Complementary mechanisms — high fan-out search is made tractable because cheap falsification prunes candidates, and both are cited as areas where AI has an advantage.
Implementation of an attribution split — the disclosure artifact is where the responsibility boundary becomes explicit and auditable.
Single-result invalidation — one algorithmic breakthrough is claimed to break all cryptocurrencies and destabilize the economy, making capability advances non-additive for security substrates.
Analogic precedent — machine superiority did not extinguish human participation, offered as the basis for expecting continued human pursuit of math and science.

evidence_quotes.text: Mathematics has rigorous, fully self-contained ways of checking validity, making it very amenable to AI training via reinforcement learning.
Theoretical physics is much less self-contained than mathematics regarding what counts as a good solution.
AI will automate formal verification much faster than domains requiring empirical or subjective validation.

core_insights.generalization: Applies to any agentic system: tasks with cheap deterministic success checks (compilers, test suites, type systems, formal specs, replayable simulations) accrue capability gains far faster than tasks whose success is a judgment call. Build the checker first; then close the loop.
core_insights.insight: The rate at which a domain gets absorbed by AI appears to be gated by the quality of its verifier — cheap, automatic, fully objective validity checking — rather than by the domain's perceived intellectual difficulty. Mathematics and theoretical CS have self-contained proof checking (Lean-style assistants) and therefore sit on the RL training loop directly; theoretical physics lacks an agreed objective notion of 'a good solution,' so impact lags behind by months.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It gives a predictive rule for where agentic capability compounding will and won't happen: look for the verifier before looking at the task. It also reframes verifier construction as the highest-leverage engineering investment, upstream of model or prompt work.

evidence_quotes.text: The search for algorithms is highly parallelizable, and AI excels at finding counterexamples and exploring search spaces.

core_insights.generalization: Agent harnesses should be designed as fan-out search with a deterministic adversarial checker at the funnel, and capacity planning should budget for verification, deduplication, and human adjudication rather than for more generation.
core_insights.insight: The AI capability that is actually being exploited is not 'reasoning' in the abstract but massively parallel candidate generation plus cheap falsification: AI's comparative advantage is exploring search spaces and finding counterexamples, and algorithm search is highly parallelizable. The bottleneck migrates from generating candidates to checking and adjudicating them.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It suggests the winning harness shape is wide parallel generation against an automated falsifier, not a single long serial chain of thought. Throughput of the checker — not the generator — determines end-to-end performance and cost.

evidence_quotes.text: There is a tension between AI generating proofs and human researchers framing, guiding, and taking responsibility for the results.
Mathematicians must adapt their research methods and focus on higher-level problem setting and narrative creation.

core_insights.generalization: In any agentic system, the human's enforced surface should be goal specification, framing constraints, and accountability — the parts that cannot be verified automatically and that carry consequences when wrong.
core_insights.insight: The human role boundary is relocating to the layer above generation: setting the research agenda, choosing framing and metaphors, and taking responsibility for results, while the AI does proof and lemma execution. The stated practical adaptation for mathematicians is precisely this move to higher-level problem setting and narrative creation.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It names the durable human interface in an agentic pipeline as the objective/reward/accountability layer rather than the artifact-production layer, which changes what tools need to expose (spec authoring, critique, ownership) and who is on the hook for failure.

evidence_quotes.text: Academic papers now frequently include AI disclosure sections at the end.
The criteria for academic credit and publishing standards need complete restructuring.

core_insights.generalization: Any pipeline where AI produces claims should carry per-claim provenance (model, prompt, verifier, human approver) as a first-class output, because the downstream review, blame, and reward systems depend on it.
core_insights.insight: AI attribution is becoming a formal artifact requirement rather than a cultural convention: papers now routinely carry AI disclosure sections, and the split being negotiated is human conceptualization versus AI execution. This implies machine-readable provenance of which agent or model produced which sub-result is a publishing requirement, which is structurally the same problem as provenance and attribution logging in multi-agent pipelines.
core_insights.why_it_matters: Credit and liability systems are the first place where AI-assisted output forces structured labeling; the same labeling discipline is what makes agent traces auditable, debuggable, and reviewable in production.

evidence_quotes.text: If P equals NP were proven by an efficient algorithm, it would be an absolute cataclysm for cryptography and the economy.
Breaking all cryptocurrencies if P equals NP with an efficient algorithm.

core_insights.generalization: Design for substrate invalidation: crypto agility, swappable verifier or oracle layers, and dependency assumptions that can be revoked quickly, because a single upstream result can retire an entire abstraction layer.
core_insights.insight: Capability gains are not additive — a single algorithmic result can discontinuously invalidate an entire deployed substrate. The concrete case given is an efficient algorithm proving P = NP, which is described as a cataclysm for cryptography and the economy (e.g. breaking all cryptocurrencies), i.e. one proof invalidates a class of security primitives that the whole system depends on.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It implies capability-tracking for AI systems must include discontinuity/invalidation playbooks, not just incremental benchmarks: some advances destroy the assumptions of previously shipped systems rather than improving them.

evidence_quotes.text: Singularity refers to a point where technological change becomes so rapid that we lose the ability to predict beyond it.

core_insights.generalization: When a dependency changes faster than your planning horizon, favor reversible, cheap-to-swap components and continuous re-benchmarking over long-horizon commitments.
core_insights.insight: The singularity framing used here is predictive-collapse, not a capability threshold: the point at which change is rapid enough that forecasting beyond it fails. That applies to planning horizons in engineering as much as to culture — roadmaps and long-lived assumptions become invalid before they can be validated.
core_insights.why_it_matters: It argues for short re-evaluation cycles and reversible architecture decisions when the environment's rate of change exceeds the evaluation horizon, which is a concrete constraint on planning cadence.

key_claims.evidence: Academic papers now frequently include AI disclosure sections at the end.

project_ideas.based_on: the winning harness shape is wide parallel generation against an automated falsifier
project_ideas.hypothesis: For a fixed compute budget on algorithm-discovery and lemma-proving tasks, a fan-out harness (N parallel candidate generators feeding a deterministic falsifier) will produce more verified artifacts per dollar than a single serial chain-of-thought baseline, and end-to-end throughput will scale with checker throughput rather than generator count above a measurable crossover point.
project_ideas.measurement: Verified artifacts per compute-dollar, funnel utilization (generated vs. checked vs. accepted candidates), and the generator-count value at which added generation stops increasing verified output.
project_ideas.name: Checker-Throughput Fan-Out Harness
project_ideas.poc: Wrap an existing formal proof assistant or compiler-grade test suite as the deterministic funnel, run identical budgets through a serial baseline and a fan-out variant, and instrument generator throughput, falsifier throughput, dedup rate, and verified-artifact yield per stage.

project_ideas.based_on: Trace capture (which model, which prompt, which verifier, which human approver) becomes a required output of the pipeline rather than optional telemetry
project_ideas.hypothesis: Attaching a per-claim provenance record (generating model, prompt or spec reference, verifier identity and result, human approver, confidence) to every AI-assisted claim materially reduces the time reviewers need to adjudicate a disputed result compared to a baseline with no provenance, and reviewers will prefer it even when it exposes lower confidence.
project_ideas.measurement: Median adjudication time per disputed claim, adjudication accuracy on injected-error cases, and reviewer-reported trust or willingness to reuse the pipeline.
project_ideas.name: Per-Claim Provenance Ledger
project_ideas.poc: Emit provenance as a first-class field from an agent pipeline, run two arms of reviewers (with and without the ledger) over a set of AI-assisted claims containing deliberately injected errors, and measure adjudication time, correctness, and confidence calibration.

project_ideas.based_on: Define an operational metric for 'domain impacted by AI' and measure the offset across several fields over time
project_ideas.hypothesis: A domain-level measure of automatic, objective, self-contained validity checking will predict a field's AI absorption order and lag better than a measure of domain difficulty, and the predicted ordering will hold across at least three fields over successive measurement waves.
project_ideas.measurement: Rank correlation between checker-availability score and observed absorption order, plus the measured lag between fields in the reported single-digit-month range.
project_ideas.name: Verifier-Readiness Index
project_ideas.poc: Operationalize self-containedness as presence and coverage of an automated checker for the domain's core artifacts, blind-scan recent field outputs for AI-assisted results and disclosure markers, and publish a ranked index alongside the difficulty-ranked comparison to test which predicts observed absorption.

project_ideas.based_on: Design for substrate invalidation: crypto agility, swappable verifier or oracle layers, and dependency assumptions that can be revoked quickly
project_ideas.hypothesis: A dependency graph over deployed security primitives, combined with a timed invalidation drill, will identify an actionable number of single-point-of-invalidation substrates that a single upstream algorithmic result could retire, and teams that run the drill will reduce swap time for a targeted primitive measurably relative to a pre-drill baseline.
project_ideas.measurement: Count of primitives whose invalidation propagates beyond one abstraction layer, containment time for the drill scenario, and reduction in swap time after remediation.
project_ideas.name: Substrate Invalidation Drill
project_ideas.poc: Graph the deployed primitives and their dependents in one system, define an invalidation scenario for each, run a timed drill in which one primitive class is assumed broken, and record how far the failure propagates before it is contained.

summary.html:
Overview

  • Speaker: Scott Aaronson
  • Channel: Ryan Peterman
  • Main topic: The impact of AI on mathematics, theoretical computer science, human value, and research methodology.
  • Purpose: To explore the implications of rapid advancements in AI on mathematical research, theoretical computer science, and the future value of human intelligence. Scott Aaronson discusses the paradigm shift in AI-driven theorem proving, mathematical research, and human intelligence. He explores whether humans have been dethroned as the primary theorem-proving entities, the concept of the 'mathocalypse', the changing nature of intellectual work, and the philosophical implications of AI models achieving mathematical milestones faster than expected.

Topic Map

The Mathocalypse and AI Theorem Proving

  • Explanation: Scott discusses how AI models are rapidly solving complex mathematical problems, changing the nature of mathematical research and challenging the human monopoly on theorem proving.
  • Key claims:
    • Humans have been dethroned as the main theorem-proving entities on Earth.
    • AI models are solving millennium problems and open problems in math, computer science, and physics at an unprecedented rate.
    • The time scale for technological breakthroughs is now measured in months rather than decades.
  • Examples:
    • AI solving the unit distance problem and the Navier-Stokes problem.
  • Terminology:
    • Mathocalypse
    • Singularity
    • Millennium problems
  • Why it matters: It marks a fundamental turning point in intellectual work where AI matches or exceeds human capabilities in formal reasoning.

Defining the Singularity in Intellectual Work

  • Explanation: Defining technological singularity in the context of intellectual work and the inability to predict technological change beyond a certain threshold.
  • Key claims:
    • Singularity refers to a point where technological change becomes so rapid that we lose the ability to predict beyond it.
    • Whether the future is utopian or dystopian, we are entering a period of vastly accelerated technological change.
  • Examples:
  • Terminology:
    • Singularity
    • Technological change
  • Why it matters: It sets the context for understanding the profound uncertainty and transformation facing researchers and society.

The Self-Contained Nature of Math vs. Physics

  • Explanation: Contrasting how mathematical proofs are self-contained and easily verified by AI versus how theoretical physics requires more subjective judgment about what counts as a valid solution.
  • Key claims:
    • Theoretical physics is much less self-contained than mathematics regarding what counts as a good solution.
    • Mathematics has rigorous, fully self-contained ways of checking validity, making it very amenable to AI training via reinforcement learning.
  • Examples:
    • Physics theories taking 6 to 12 months longer to be impacted by AI compared to math.
  • Terminology:
    • Self-contained
    • Verification
  • Why it matters: It explains why mathematics and theoretical computer science are experiencing the AI disruption faster and more cleanly than other empirical sciences.

AI Disclosures and Attribution in Research Papers

  • Explanation: Discussing the new norms around AI disclosures in academic papers and the tension around who gets credit when AI assists or derives proofs.
  • Key claims:
    • Academic papers now frequently include AI disclosure sections at the end.
    • There is a tension between AI generating proofs and human researchers framing, guiding, and taking responsibility for the results.
  • Examples:
    • Papers where AI suggests solutions or proves lemmas while humans guide the high-level agenda.
  • Terminology:
    • AI disclosure
    • Attribution
  • Why it matters: It highlights how academic publishing norms and credit systems are having to adapt to AI-generated research.

P versus NP and Its Potential Impact

  • Explanation: Discussing the P versus NP problem, how AI might solve it, and what an algorithmic breakthrough would mean for cryptography and economics.
  • Key claims:
    • If P equals NP were proven by an efficient algorithm, it would be an absolute cataclysm for cryptography and the economy.
    • The search for algorithms is highly parallelizable, and AI excels at finding counterexamples and exploring search spaces.
  • Examples:
    • Breaking all cryptocurrencies if P equals NP with an efficient algorithm.
  • Terminology:
    • P versus NP
    • Cryptocurrency
    • Market crash
  • Why it matters: It illustrates the extreme theoretical and practical stakes of AI solving fundamental computer science problems.

Human Motivation and the Meaning of Life

  • Explanation: Exploring why humans pursue intellectual and creative endeavors even when machines can do them, drawing parallels to chess and literature.
  • Key claims:
    • Chess has never been more popular despite AI surpassing humans decades ago.
    • Humans derive meaning from relationships, creative pursuits, and the joy of participation rather than just being the absolute best at a task.
  • Examples:
    • Magnus Carlsen playing chess in a world where AI dominates chess players.
  • Terminology:
    • Chess
    • Deep Blue
    • Kasparov
  • Why it matters: It provides a hopeful perspective on human purpose and motivation in a post-AGI world.

Key Points

Human Dethronement in Theorem Proving

  • Explanation: AI models have surpassed human capabilities in proving theorems for specific mathematical domains over the summer.
  • Evidence: Solving millennium problems and open math/physics problems within months.
  • Practical implication: Mathematicians must adapt their research methods and focus on higher-level problem setting and narrative creation.

Self-Contained Nature of Mathematics

  • Explanation: Math is uniquely suited for AI because proofs can be automatically and rigorously checked without empirical ambiguity.
  • Evidence: Lean proof assistants and automated verification systems.
  • Practical implication: AI will automate formal verification much faster than domains requiring empirical or subjective validation.

The Shift in Publishing and Credit

  • Explanation: Academic norms are shifting toward AI disclosures, raising questions about authorship and attribution.
  • Evidence: AI disclosure sections appearing at the ends of research papers.
  • Practical implication: The criteria for academic credit and publishing standards need complete restructuring.

The Resilience of Human Curiosity

  • Explanation: Just as chess remained popular after AI beat human champions, human intellectual pursuits will persist out of intrinsic motivation.
  • Evidence: The boom in chess streaming and competitive play post-Deep Blue.
  • Practical implication: People will continue studying math, science, and art because they enjoy the journey, not just the destination.

Frameworks, Models & Processes

AI Attribution and Authorship Framework

  • How it works: A structured way to evaluate who gets credit when AI assists in research: human conceptualization vs. AI execution.
  • Components:
    • Setting the research agenda and metaphors
    • AI-assisted proof generation and counterexample searching
    • Human verification and formal certification
    • AI disclosure in publications
  • When to use: When writing and publishing academic research involving AI tools.

Examples & Case Studies

AI models solving the Navier-Stokes and unit distance problems within months.

  • Illustrates: The rapid acceleration of automated problem-solving in advanced mathematics.
  • Lesson: Milestone mathematical problems are falling to AI far quicker than human experts predicted.

Chess popularity exploding after Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov.

  • Illustrates: Human interest in a domain does not die when AI surpasses human skill.
  • Lesson: Competition and intrinsic enjoyment drive human endeavors independently of machine superiority.

Twitter user posting an AI-generated Monet painting and letting art critics dissect its flaws before revealing it was AI.

  • Illustrates: The bias and readiness of human critics to dismiss AI work using pseudo-intellectual critique.
  • Lesson: People often project preconceived notions and biases onto AI creations until they know the source.

Actionable Takeaways

  • Immediate:
    • Expect AI to accelerate solution timelines for math and computer science problems from decades to months.
    • Incorporate AI disclosure practices in technical writing and research publications.
  • Strategic:
    • Focus human effort on agenda setting, framing problems, and interpreting meaning rather than rote computation.
    • Recognize that intrinsic motivation and the journey of learning will sustain human disciplines like math and art.
  • Questions to investigate:
    • What are the new rules of academic credit when AI assists in major theorems?
    • How will the economic value of human intelligence shift as AI capabilities scale?

## Overview
- **Speaker**: Scott Aaronson
- **Channel**: Ryan Peterman
- **Main topic**: The impact of AI on mathematics, theoretical computer science, human value, and research methodology.
- **Purpose**: To explore the implications of rapid advancements in AI on mathematical research, theoretical computer science, and the future value of human intelligence.
Scott Aaronson discusses the paradigm shift in AI-driven theorem proving, mathematical research, and human intelligence. He explores whether humans have been dethroned as the primary theorem-proving entities, the concept of the 'mathocalypse', the changing nature of intellectual work, and the philosophical implications of AI models achieving mathematical milestones faster than expected.
## Topic Map
### The Mathocalypse and AI Theorem Proving
- **Explanation**: Scott discusses how AI models are rapidly solving complex mathematical problems, changing the nature of mathematical research and challenging the human monopoly on theorem proving.
- **Key claims**:
  - Humans have been dethroned as the main theorem-proving entities on Earth.
  - AI models are solving millennium problems and open problems in math, computer science, and physics at an unprecedented rate.
  - The time scale for technological breakthroughs is now measured in months rather than decades.
- **Examples**:
  - AI solving the unit distance problem and the Navier-Stokes problem.
- **Terminology**:
  - Mathocalypse
  - Singularity
  - Millennium problems
- **Why it matters**: It marks a fundamental turning point in intellectual work where AI matches or exceeds human capabilities in formal reasoning.
### Defining the Singularity in Intellectual Work
- **Explanation**: Defining technological singularity in the context of intellectual work and the inability to predict technological change beyond a certain threshold.
- **Key claims**:
  - Singularity refers to a point where technological change becomes so rapid that we lose the ability to predict beyond it.
  - Whether the future is utopian or dystopian, we are entering a period of vastly accelerated technological change.
- **Examples**:
- **Terminology**:
  - Singularity
  - Technological change
- **Why it matters**: It sets the context for understanding the profound uncertainty and transformation facing researchers and society.
### The Self-Contained Nature of Math vs. Physics
- **Explanation**: Contrasting how mathematical proofs are self-contained and easily verified by AI versus how theoretical physics requires more subjective judgment about what counts as a valid solution.
- **Key claims**:
  - Theoretical physics is much less self-contained than mathematics regarding what counts as a good solution.
  - Mathematics has rigorous, fully self-contained ways of checking validity, making it very amenable to AI training via reinforcement learning.
- **Examples**:
  - Physics theories taking 6 to 12 months longer to be impacted by AI compared to math.
- **Terminology**:
  - Self-contained
  - Verification
- **Why it matters**: It explains why mathematics and theoretical computer science are experiencing the AI disruption faster and more cleanly than other empirical sciences.
### AI Disclosures and Attribution in Research Papers
- **Explanation**: Discussing the new norms around AI disclosures in academic papers and the tension around who gets credit when AI assists or derives proofs.
- **Key claims**:
  - Academic papers now frequently include AI disclosure sections at the end.
  - There is a tension between AI generating proofs and human researchers framing, guiding, and taking responsibility for the results.
- **Examples**:
  - Papers where AI suggests solutions or proves lemmas while humans guide the high-level agenda.
- **Terminology**:
  - AI disclosure
  - Attribution
- **Why it matters**: It highlights how academic publishing norms and credit systems are having to adapt to AI-generated research.
### P versus NP and Its Potential Impact
- **Explanation**: Discussing the P versus NP problem, how AI might solve it, and what an algorithmic breakthrough would mean for cryptography and economics.
- **Key claims**:
  - If P equals NP were proven by an efficient algorithm, it would be an absolute cataclysm for cryptography and the economy.
  - The search for algorithms is highly parallelizable, and AI excels at finding counterexamples and exploring search spaces.
- **Examples**:
  - Breaking all cryptocurrencies if P equals NP with an efficient algorithm.
- **Terminology**:
  - P versus NP
  - Cryptocurrency
  - Market crash
- **Why it matters**: It illustrates the extreme theoretical and practical stakes of AI solving fundamental computer science problems.
### Human Motivation and the Meaning of Life
- **Explanation**: Exploring why humans pursue intellectual and creative endeavors even when machines can do them, drawing parallels to chess and literature.
- **Key claims**:
  - Chess has never been more popular despite AI surpassing humans decades ago.
  - Humans derive meaning from relationships, creative pursuits, and the joy of participation rather than just being the absolute best at a task.
- **Examples**:
  - Magnus Carlsen playing chess in a world where AI dominates chess players.
- **Terminology**:
  - Chess
  - Deep Blue
  - Kasparov
- **Why it matters**: It provides a hopeful perspective on human purpose and motivation in a post-AGI world.
## Key Points
### Human Dethronement in Theorem Proving
- **Explanation**: AI models have surpassed human capabilities in proving theorems for specific mathematical domains over the summer.
- **Evidence**: Solving millennium problems and open math/physics problems within months.
- **Practical implication**: Mathematicians must adapt their research methods and focus on higher-level problem setting and narrative creation.
### Self-Contained Nature of Mathematics
- **Explanation**: Math is uniquely suited for AI because proofs can be automatically and rigorously checked without empirical ambiguity.
- **Evidence**: Lean proof assistants and automated verification systems.
- **Practical implication**: AI will automate formal verification much faster than domains requiring empirical or subjective validation.
### The Shift in Publishing and Credit
- **Explanation**: Academic norms are shifting toward AI disclosures, raising questions about authorship and attribution.
- **Evidence**: AI disclosure sections appearing at the ends of research papers.
- **Practical implication**: The criteria for academic credit and publishing standards need complete restructuring.
### The Resilience of Human Curiosity
- **Explanation**: Just as chess remained popular after AI beat human champions, human intellectual pursuits will persist out of intrinsic motivation.
- **Evidence**: The boom in chess streaming and competitive play post-Deep Blue.
- **Practical implication**: People will continue studying math, science, and art because they enjoy the journey, not just the destination.
## Frameworks, Models & Processes
### AI Attribution and Authorship Framework
- **How it works**: A structured way to evaluate who gets credit when AI assists in research: human conceptualization vs. AI execution.
- **Components**:
  - Setting the research agenda and metaphors
  - AI-assisted proof generation and counterexample searching
  - Human verification and formal certification
  - AI disclosure in publications
- **When to use**: When writing and publishing academic research involving AI tools.
## Examples & Case Studies
### AI models solving the Navier-Stokes and unit distance problems within months.
- **Illustrates**: The rapid acceleration of automated problem-solving in advanced mathematics.
- **Lesson**: Milestone mathematical problems are falling to AI far quicker than human experts predicted.
### Chess popularity exploding after Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov.
- **Illustrates**: Human interest in a domain does not die when AI surpasses human skill.
- **Lesson**: Competition and intrinsic enjoyment drive human endeavors independently of machine superiority.
### Twitter user posting an AI-generated Monet painting and letting art critics dissect its flaws before revealing it was AI.
- **Illustrates**: The bias and readiness of human critics to dismiss AI work using pseudo-intellectual critique.
- **Lesson**: People often project preconceived notions and biases onto AI creations until they know the source.
## Actionable Takeaways
- **Immediate**:
  - Expect AI to accelerate solution timelines for math and computer science problems from decades to months.
  - Incorporate AI disclosure practices in technical writing and research publications.
- **Strategic**:
  - Focus human effort on agenda setting, framing problems, and interpreting meaning rather than rote computation.
  - Recognize that intrinsic motivation and the journey of learning will sustain human disciplines like math and art.
- **Questions to investigate**:
  - What are the new rules of academic credit when AI assists in major theorems?
  - How will the economic value of human intelligence shift as AI capabilities scale?
## Claims Worth Verifying

- Chess popularity increased after Deep Blue defeated Kasparov. (historical)

> "One needs to be a particular kind of idiot to not deny what's going on now." (at 2:01)
